In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the selectivity of NPP and alkaline phosphatases for monoesters and diesters, respectively, is determined by the combined contributions of the charge of the substrate oxygen atoms that contact the metal ions, and by the electrostatic and steric interactions of substrate oxygen atoms that are not coordinated to Zn(2+).
the two enzymes achieve high selectivity by different means.

the NPP active site has been engineered by evolution to be more permissive to noncognate substrate binding, and this permissive nature of the site is the basis for its ability to hydrolyze a broader range of substrates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NPP is more tolerant of charge changes in the nonbridging oxygens in its substrates than is alkaline phosphatases.
NPP and alkaline phosphatases are structurally similar enzymes, but the former is a more flexible enzyme that is able to hydrolyze a wider range of substrates.
the selectivity of NPP and alkaline phosphatases is achieved through a combination of electrostatics and steric effects that are tuned to the specific substrates of the enzymes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the two phosphatases achieve their selectivity through different mechanisms, which may have implications for engineering enzymes for new activities and/or improved catalytic proficiency.
the selectivity of NPP and alkaline phosphatases for monoester versus diester substrates is not determined solely through the electrostatics of the active site.

the alkaline phosphodiesterase and alkaline phosphatases represent a family that has evolved from a common ancestor to hydrolyze different classes of substrates, and that the two enzymes are not so far apart in their active site chemistry to prevent the promiscuous activity that we observe in NPP.
